column1: sit down|sitting,chair|Is this seat free?~Yes. Please sit down.~Am I early?~Only a little. We can have tea while we wait.|Invite a visitor to take a seat without sounding like a command.|Please sit down. Would you like some tea?|Use sit down for the action of taking a seat. Be seated describes the resulting position and can sound more formal.

pick up|lifting,helping|Can you pick up that box?~Yes. Where should I put it?~On the table, please.~I will hold it from underneath.|Replace the box with it: Please pick up the box.|Please pick it up.|Separable in this sense: pick the box up / pick up the box; pick it up. The meaning here is lifting, not collecting someone.

get ready|clothes,morning|Are you ready to leave?~Not yet. I need to get ready.~What do you still need?~My coat and my keys.|You have your shoes on but cannot find your keys. Say what you still need to do before leaving.|I still need to find my keys before I am ready to leave.|Get ready describes preparing yourself; be ready describes the state after preparation.

find out|dictionary,document|Do children need a ticket?~I do not know. I will find out.~Could you check the age limit too?~Yes. I will ask the organizer.|You need the event's age limit and ticket rule. Write one specific question to find out both.|What is the age limit, and do children need a ticket?|Find out usually means discovering information. Use find for locating a physical object: find the keys.

work out|puzzle,notebook|We have twelve guests and three tables.~Can we work out a seating plan?~Four people at each table would fit.~Let us check whether the chairs are available.|There are twelve guests and three equal tables. Work out a plan and state what else must be checked.|Seat four guests at each table and check that twelve suitable chairs are available.|Work something out means solve or calculate it here. It is separable: work the answer out / work it out.

look into|document,library|The return journey looks expensive.~Could we look into another route?~I will compare the bus and the train.~Please check the last departure, not just the fare.|Before replacing a train with a bus, identify two things to look into.|The fare and the time of the last departure.|Look into means investigate here. It is inseparable: look into it, not look it into.

follow through|checklist,community|The group agreed to repair the gate.~Has anyone followed through?~A volunteer ordered the parts, and the work is booked for Friday.~Then the promise has turned into an actual arrangement.|Which better demonstrates following through: suggesting a repair or booking the work after agreeing to arrange it? Explain.|Booking the work shows action that carries the agreement forward.|Follow through on a promise or commitment. Distinguish taking the first step from carrying the task to completion.

weigh up|budget,map|Would you choose the cheaper venue?~I need to weigh up the savings against the longer journey.~The other one is easier to reach.~And that could affect who is able to attend.|Compare two venues: one is cheaper; one is easier to reach. Give a balanced recommendation using weigh up.|We should weigh up the savings against access before choosing the venue.|Weigh up the options / weigh the options up; weigh them up. Common in British English; weigh the options is also natural.

factor in|map,clock|Leaving at seven twenty should be fine.~Have you factored in the fifteen-minute walk?~I had not. There is a ten-minute queue as well.~Then we should work backward from the seven-thirty start.|A walk starts at 7:30. Allow fifteen minutes to get there and ten minutes to enter. Give the latest departure time and explain.|Leave by 7:05 after factoring in both the walk and the queue.|Separable: factor the delay in / factor in the delay; factor it in. Include a relevant time, cost or condition in a calculation.

iron out|strategy,whiteboard|Two volunteers have the early shift, but nobody has closing.~We need to iron that out before sending the rota.~I can move to the late shift if someone covers the first half hour.~I will cover it. That leaves us staffed throughout.|Replace We will deal with it with a specific update about an empty closing shift, using iron out.|We have ironed out the gap by moving one volunteer to closing and arranging cover for the first half hour.|Separable: iron out the problems / iron the problems out; iron them out. Resolve difficulties rather than simply discover them.

bear out|document,notebook|Did attendance rise after the timetable changed?~The figures do not bear out that claim.~Perhaps the change helped a different group?~Possibly, but we would need evidence before saying so.|A report claims attendance increased, but the count stayed level. Rewrite its conclusion using bear out.|The attendance figures do not bear out the claim that participation increased.|Evidence bears out a claim; the claim is what is supported. Separable: bear the claim out / bear it out.

dispense with|minimal,document|Do we need another approval form?~If it serves no useful purpose, we can dispense with it.~Would that remove the safety check too?~No. We should remove duplication, not the check itself.|Distinguish dispensing with a duplicate form from abandoning an essential check.|The duplicate paperwork can be removed while the necessary check remains.|Dispense with is inseparable: dispense with it. It means manage without or remove something regarded as unnecessary.

come in|room,chair|Shall I wait outside?~No. Please come in.~Where should I put my bag?~Beside the chair is fine.|Welcome a visitor and tell them where to put their bag.|Please come in. You can put your bag beside the chair.|Come in invites entry toward the speaker. Go in describes entry viewed from elsewhere.

bring along|bag,water|Do I need to buy lunch?~No. Bring along a sandwich.~Should I bring water too?~Yes. We may be outside for a while.|Invite a friend on a walk and name two things to bring along.|Bring along a sandwich and some water.|Bring along a friend or an item. With a pronoun: bring it along, not bring along it.

take turns|sharing,guitar|We both want to use the guitar.~We can take turns.~Who goes first?~You can play one song, then I will.|Two people want one guitar. Suggest a fair arrangement using take turns.|We can take turns playing one song each.|Take turns doing something, or take turns to do it. Taking turns means alternating, not doing the action simultaneously.

map out|itinerary,whiteboard|Shall we start designing the signs?~Let us map out the visitor's route first.~From the entrance to the exit?~Yes, including the points where someone might need help.|Before designing signs, identify two parts of a visitor's route worth mapping out.|Where visitors enter and where they must choose between different directions.|Map out is separable: map the route out / map it out. It can refer to a detailed plan, not only a physical map.

check in with|phone,listening|Has the new volunteer settled in?~I will check in with her after the first session.~Are you expecting a formal report?~No. A short conversation about what she needs.|Write a brief message checking in with a new volunteer without demanding a report.|How did the first session go? Is there anything you need before the next one?|Check in with someone means contact them briefly here. It differs from checking in at a hotel.

account for|calendar,budget|The schedule leaves no time for questions.~Then it does not account for how the workshop actually works.~Could we shorten the opening talk?~Yes, and reserve time for discussion.|Adjust a workshop schedule to account for questions without making it longer.|Shorten the introduction and reserve the saved time for questions.|Account for means allow for or consider here. In another sense, account for a delay means explain it; keep the intended sense clear.

build on|notebook,strategy|Should we discard last month's feedback?~The new proposal should build on it.~Even the comments that challenge our idea?~Those may be the most useful starting point.|Explain how a revised proposal can build on criticism rather than merely repeat the first proposal.|Use the criticism to identify a weakness and develop a concrete change addressing it.|Build on is inseparable: build on it. It uses an existing idea, resource or achievement as a basis for development.

bear on|document,city|Why include the site's earlier use in this discussion?~It bears directly on who can use the entrance now.~Then it is relevant to the current decision?~Yes, rather than just an interesting historical aside.|Does a fact bear on a decision merely because it is interesting? Explain.|No. It must be relevant to, or affect, the matter being considered.|Bear on means be relevant to or affect. Do not confuse it with bear out, which means support a claim.

hold in tension|discussion,strategy|Can we resolve openness and privacy with a single rule?~We may need to hold them in tension.~Rather than declare one value irrelevant?~Yes. The arrangement must remain answerable to both.|Describe a choice that holds openness and privacy in tension without dismissing either.|Publish useful information about the event while protecting participants' private details.|Hold two values in tension recognizes their competing claims without pretending the difficulty has disappeared.

wake up|alarm,morning|What time do you wake up?~At seven.~Do you get out of bed at once?~Not always. Sometimes I stay there for a few minutes.|Can someone wake up before getting out of bed? Explain.|Yes. Waking up means stopping sleeping; getting up means leaving the bed.|Wake up and get up are related but not identical. A person can be awake while still in bed.

put on|coat,clothes|It is cold outside.~I will put on my coat.~Do you need a scarf too?~Yes, please. The wind is strong.|Replace my coat with it: I will put on my coat.|I will put it on.|Separable: put the coat on / put on the coat; put it on. Wear describes having the clothing on, not the action of dressing.

slow down|walk,clock|I cannot keep up.~I will slow down.~Thank you. I want to look at the buildings too.~Then we do not need to hurry.|A companion cannot keep up during a walk. Respond with an appropriate offer.|I will slow down. We do not need to hurry.|Slow down can describe movement or the pace of an activity. Slow someone down means cause them to move or progress less quickly.

make time for|calendar,walk|You keep postponing the walk.~I need to make time for it rather than wait for a free afternoon.~Would ten minutes after lunch work?~Yes. I can put that in the calendar.|Turn I will walk when I am free into a specific plan that makes time for it.|I will take ten minutes after lunch for a short walk.|Make time for a person or activity; make time to do something. It implies arranging priorities, not creating extra hours.

cut back on|phone,budget|You have left the phone in another room.~I am trying to cut back on checking it during dinner.~Will you stop using it altogether?~No. I just want fewer interruptions.|Explain why cutting back on phone use does not necessarily mean giving it up completely.|It means reducing the amount or frequency rather than necessarily stopping.|Cut back on + noun or -ing form. The expression is not separable: cut back on it.

stick to|calendar,checklist|Your reading plan looks modest.~That is why I think I can stick to it.~What happens on a busy day?~I will read one page rather than abandon the habit.|Suggest a fallback that helps someone stick to reading without demanding the same amount every day.|Read at least one page on busy days and return to the longer session when possible.|Stick to a plan or decision means continue following it. A realistic adjustment need not mean abandoning the underlying commitment.

set aside|notebook,saving|When will you prepare the talk?~I have set aside twenty minutes this afternoon.~Will messages interrupt you?~I will silence them for that period.|Reserve a specific amount of time for a task using set aside.|I will set aside twenty minutes this afternoon to prepare the talk.|Separable: set aside the time / set the time aside; set it aside. State what the reserved resource is for.

get around to|book,notebook|Have you sorted the photographs yet?~I finally got around to it yesterday.~What made it possible?~I stopped waiting for a whole free weekend.|Explain what finally suggests in I finally got around to sorting the photographs.|The task had been intended or postponed for some time before it was done.|Get around to + noun or -ing: get around to sorting, not get around to sort. British English also uses get round to.

default to|phone,minimal|What happens when the schedule becomes unclear?~I default to checking messages.~Does that help decide what matters next?~Usually not. It simply fills the gap with a familiar action.|Identify the automatic choice in I default to checking messages whenever I feel uncertain.|Checking messages becomes the familiar option without a deliberate decision.|Default to + noun or -ing form. It describes the option adopted automatically when an alternative is not actively selected.

carve out|calendar,relaxing|How did you find an hour for writing?~I carved it out by moving two optional meetings.~Then it was not simply unused time?~No. I had to protect it from other demands.|Distinguish carving out time from happening to have nothing scheduled.|Carving out time involves securing it despite competing demands.|Separable: carve out an hour / carve an hour out. Often used for securing time, space or an opportunity with effort.

make allowance for|clock,calendar|The route estimate assumes everyone walks at the same pace.~We should make allowance for slower walkers.~Would an extra ten minutes be enough?~Let us ask the group before fixing the departure time.|Explain why making allowance for different walking speeds can improve an estimate.|It recognizes a relevant difference instead of treating one pace as universal.|Make allowance for a circumstance means adjust a judgment or arrangement in recognition of it; it need not excuse every outcome.

stand back from|notebook,relaxing|We have changed the tracker three times this week.~Perhaps we should stand back from the routine itself.~And ask what it is meant to support?~Yes. We are improving the instrument without examining the purpose.|Suggest a question that helps someone stand back from a routine they keep optimizing.|What valuable activity is this routine actually meant to support?|Stand back from is figurative here: gain perspective rather than remain absorbed in immediate details.

a helping hand|helping,lifting|This box is too heavy for me.~Would you like a helping hand?~Yes. Could you hold this end?~Of course. Lift on three.|Offer a helping hand and ask where your help is needed.|Would you like a helping hand? Which end should I hold?|A helping hand means assistance, not an additional physical hand. Common verbs: give, lend, need.

take your time|relaxing,book|I have not finished reading the instructions.~Take your time. We are not starting yet.~Can I ask you about the last step?~Yes. Let us read it together.|A beginner is rushing through instructions. Reassure them using take your time.|Take your time. We can read the last step together.|Take your time reassures someone that they need not hurry. In a critical tone, taking your time can imply delay; tone matters.

on the same page|strategy,document|I thought we were meeting at the library.~I meant the cafe beside it.~Let us make sure we are on the same page before telling the others.~The cafe, at ten, by the window.|A meeting message names two different places. Rewrite it to put everyone on the same page.|We are meeting at the cafe beside the library at ten, by the window.|Informal and figurative: sharing an understanding, not necessarily complete agreement on every issue.

a piece of cake|puzzle,checklist|Was assembling the shelf difficult?~The first part was a piece of cake.~And the last part?~That needed two people to hold it level.|Does The first part was a piece of cake prove the whole job was easy? Explain.|No. It describes only the first part as very easy.|Informal. Be careful about calling another person's difficult task a piece of cake; it can sound dismissive.

play it by ear|map,rain|Should we reserve every hour of Saturday?~Let us book the train and play the afternoon by ear.~What if it rains?~We can choose an indoor activity when we see the weather.|Make a plan that includes one fixed arrangement and one part to play by ear.|Book the return train, then choose the afternoon activity according to the weather.|Decide as circumstances develop. Distinguish this figurative use from playing music by ear without reading a score.

get the ball rolling|whiteboard,notebook|Nobody seems ready to speak.~I can get the ball rolling with one question.~Which one?~What made the last workshop difficult to join?|Write one concrete opening question to get a planning discussion started.|What made the last workshop difficult for newcomers to join?|An informal way to say start an activity or process. A small first action can get the ball rolling.

strike a balance|calendar,sharing|Do we need a timetable for every conversation?~We should strike a balance between structure and free time.~What would that look like?~Fixed meal times, with an open afternoon.|Propose a balance between planning and flexibility for a day trip.|Fix the travel times but leave the afternoon activity optional.|Common pattern: strike a balance between A and B. It need not mean dividing resources exactly in half.

leave no stone unturned|library,document|Have we checked every source for the missing record?~The archive, the old catalog and the local collection.~Then we really have left no stone unturned.~We should still state that the record has not been found.|Does leaving no stone unturned guarantee finding an answer? Explain.|No. It describes a thorough search, not a guaranteed result.|A figurative expression for trying every reasonable avenue. Avoid using it to imply certainty about the result.

the devil is in the details|document,checklist|Entry is free, so we can register when we arrive.~Read the conditions. Registration closes at noon.~The devil is in the details. I only noticed free entry.~We still have time to register now.|Which overlooked detail matters: the poster's color or a registration deadline six hours before the contest? Explain.|The deadline matters because someone arriving without registering earlier may be unable to enter.|A warning about overlooked implementation details. Use a concrete consequential detail rather than a purely decorative preference.

a double-edged sword|phone,discussion|The photos brought in many more visitors.~Publicity can be a double-edged sword.~Because guests may not want their faces online?~Exactly. We should ask before sharing identifiable images.|Name both edges of a public event hashtag: one benefit and one related drawback.|It can help people discover the event, yet expose participants' images to strangers.|Name a benefit and a cost of the same thing. Two unrelated complaints do not illustrate the idiom.

cut the Gordian knot|strategy,document|The committee keeps arguing over twenty overlapping rules.~Could one clear access policy cut the Gordian knot?~Perhaps, if it removes duplication without hiding the real conflicts.~Then we should test what the simpler rule actually settles.|Does cutting the Gordian knot always mean ignoring important complexity? Explain.|No. It means a decisive solution to a tangled problem, but whether it is justified depends on what it resolves or overlooks.|A literary allusion to a decisive solution. More formal than sort it out; not simply any small adjustment.

a curate’s egg|room,book|Was the exhibition worth visiting?~It was a curate's egg: excellent objects, but confusing explanations.~Would you still recommend it?~For the objects, yes, with that reservation.|Assess a workshop with excellent demonstrations but poor access information using a curate's egg.|The workshop was a curate's egg: the demonstrations were excellent, but the access information was poor.|Chiefly British; partly good and partly bad. Its historical irony can make it sound wry or mildly critical.

a big help|helping,checklist|I labeled the boxes for you.~That is a big help.~Do you need anything else?~Could you put the empty ones by the door?|Thank someone and identify what made their action a big help.|Labeling the boxes was a big help; now I can find the right materials quickly.|A big help can refer to a person, an action or a thing. Explain the benefit to make thanks specific.

no problem|serving,helping|Could you move this chair for me?~No problem. Where would you like it?~By the window, please.~There you are.|Respond helpfully to a request to move a chair and ask where it should go.|No problem. Where would you like it?|An informal reply to a request or thanks. It signals willingness; it does not necessarily describe the task's objective difficulty.

lend a hand|helping,community|Could anyone lend a hand with the tables?~I can help for fifteen minutes.~That is enough to move these two.~Then let us start with the one near the door.|Offer to lend a hand while giving a clear limit on your availability.|I can lend a hand for fifteen minutes. Which table should we move first?|Figurative: lend a hand means help. It does not imply a later repayment of the same kind.

pull your weight|community,sharing|I have done the shopping and the washing-up this week.~You are right. I have not been pulling my weight.~Could you take responsibility for dinner tomorrow?~Yes. I will plan it and clear up afterward.|Replace a vague promise to pull your weight with one specific responsibility.|I will prepare dinner tomorrow and clear up afterward.|An informal expression about doing a fair share. It can sound accusatory; specify the imbalance and a workable change.

many hands make light work|community,helping|We still have forty chairs to move.~With four people, we can each take a section.~Many hands make light work.~As long as we agree where the chairs are going.|Does adding helpers always make a task easier? Name a condition that helps the proverb apply.|Helpers need enough space, a shared plan and tasks they can usefully divide.|A proverb about shared effort. Coordination still matters; more people do not automatically improve every task.

iron out the wrinkles|strategy,checklist|The main plan is agreed, but two delivery times overlap.~We can iron out the wrinkles before Friday.~Who will call the supplier?~I will, and then send an updated timetable.|Identify a wrinkle in an otherwise agreed plan and propose a precise fix.|Two delivery times overlap; confirm a new slot with one supplier and update the timetable.|Figurative wrinkles are remaining practical problems. The expression usually suggests adjustments rather than a complete redesign.

see the wood for the trees|whiteboard,notebook|We have spent an hour comparing fonts.~Are we losing the ability to see the wood for the trees?~Perhaps. The real question is whether people can find the entrance.~Then let us test the sign on the street.|A team debates fonts while visitors cannot find the door. Identify the larger issue they are overlooking.|Whether the sign helps visitors locate the entrance.|Chiefly British; American English commonly uses see the forest for the trees. Both contrast detail with the larger picture.

meet halfway|discussion,map|I cannot leave as early as you want.~Could we meet halfway and take the ten-thirty train?~That would let me finish work first.~And still give us an afternoon at the coast.|Suggest a compromise between a ten o'clock departure and an eleven o'clock departure.|Could we meet halfway and leave at ten thirty?|Figurative meeting halfway means mutual compromise. It need not concern a geographical midpoint.

move the goalposts|document,strategy|We submitted the design against the agreed criteria.~Now they want a different size and an additional room.~That feels like moving the goalposts.~We should ask whether the new requirements will change the deadline.|Explain why adding new criteria after submission may be described as moving the goalposts.|The standards for success change after people have already worked toward the original ones.|Usually critical: changing the requirements in a way that makes success harder or less predictable.

the devil is in the detail|document,checklist|The agreement sounds straightforward.~Check the cancellation clause before we accept it.~The devil is in the detail, then?~Yes. The deposit is refundable only until tomorrow.|Why is a refund deadline a relevant example of this idiom?|A small contractual condition can have a substantial practical consequence.|A variant of the devil is in the details. Either form needs a consequential detail, not a trivial observation.

so far, so good|notebook,plant|How is your new routine going?~So far, so good.~Have you tried it on a busy day yet?~Not yet. That will be the real test.|Does So far, so good promise that future results will also be good? Explain.|No. It says things have gone well up to the present point.|A cautious positive report about progress to date, not a guarantee about the future.

step by step|growth,checklist|I cannot build the whole shelf today.~We can do it step by step.~What comes first?~Sorting the parts before fixing the frame.|Break a shelving task into two sensible steps.|First sort the parts; then assemble the frame.|Doing a task through ordered stages. Identify the steps rather than using the phrase as vague encouragement.

less is more|minimal,room|Shall we add three more signs?~One clear sign may be enough. Less is more.~Only if people can actually see it.~Agreed. Simplicity still needs to work.|Explain when removing extra signs could improve a space and when it could make it worse.|It helps if it reduces confusion while preserving clear guidance; it hurts if essential directions disappear.|A saying favoring effective simplicity. It does not establish that fewer elements are always better.

a fresh start|notebook,morning|My old study plan has fallen apart.~Would a fresh start help?~Yes, but I do not want another impossible promise.~Then begin with a small plan you can keep.|Propose a fresh start after an unrealistic reading target fails.|Begin with ten minutes a day and review the plan after a week.|A new beginning, often after difficulty. A fresh start can retain what was learned rather than erase the past.

break the ice|sharing,tea|Nobody at the table knows one another.~I might ask about the books people brought.~That could break the ice.~And give everyone an easy way into the conversation.|Choose an opening question for strangers that is easy to answer and not intrusive.|What brought you to today's book swap?|An informal expression for easing initial social awkwardness, not forcing private disclosure.

spread yourself too thin|calendar,checklist|You have promised to run four new activities.~I may be spreading myself too thin.~Which commitment could someone else take?~I will ask the group before I agree to anything more.|Name one practical response to being spread too thin.|Renegotiate one commitment or delegate a clearly defined task before taking on more work.|Taking on more commitments than you can give adequate attention to. It concerns limited capacity, not simply being busy.

a change of pace|walk,plant|You usually spend Sunday at your desk.~An afternoon in the garden would be a change of pace.~Would it have to be productive?~No. Doing something different would be enough.|Suggest a change of pace for someone who has spent the week indoors at a desk.|A gentle walk or an afternoon in the garden.|A different activity or rhythm, often welcome. It need not be faster, more difficult or more productive.

go through the motions|phone,document|You attend every meeting but hardly remember the discussion.~I think I have been going through the motions.~Would changing your role help?~Perhaps, but first I need to decide whether the meetings serve a useful purpose.|Distinguish going through the motions from being actively engaged.|The outward activity is performed without genuine attention, interest or commitment.|Usually critical or self-critical. It describes mechanical participation, not merely following a necessary procedure carefully.

lose sight of|calendar,notebook|The hobby now has weekly performance targets.~Have we lost sight of why we began?~We wanted to enjoy making things together.~Then the targets should support that rather than replace it.|A hobby becomes stressful because every session is measured. Identify what participants may have lost sight of.|The enjoyment or shared activity that originally motivated the hobby.|Lose sight of is figurative here: stop keeping a purpose or fact in mind. It does not require literal loss of vision.

the tail wagging the dog|phone,clock|The tracker says I should walk another kilometer.~But you planned a short walk with a friend.~The tail is wagging the dog if the number dictates the whole outing.~Then decide what the walk is for before following the display.|Identify the tail and the dog when a tracking target overrides a walk intended for conversation.|The metric is the secondary tool; the shared walk and its purpose are the larger activity it should serve.|A secondary element controls the larger purpose it is meant to support. Name both to make the metaphor precise.

leave well enough alone|plant,relaxing|The routine finally feels manageable.~Are you going to optimize it again?~I think I will leave well enough alone.~Then you can spend the time enjoying what it supports.|Explain why leaving well enough alone need not mean refusing every improvement.|It can be a judgment that an already satisfactory arrangement does not need further intervention now.|Often advice against unnecessary change. American English; British English also uses leave well alone.
